title: The Sun and the Night as Visible Mysteries of Light and Darkness
arc: The teaching reads the daily round of sun and night as a public correspondence: the sun reveals in the cosmos the unburied Father of Greatness in his light, beauty, peace, releasing-power and life-giving influx, while the night reveals as shadow the mystery of darkness — so that the two luminaries together stand as the two visible mysteries by which heaven and hell are made daily legible in the natural.
reading:
This teaching is a sustained meditation on the sun and the night as the two great visible signs that the cosmos itself preaches daily. It is structured as a doubled enumeration: first the evils that the night does, then the goods that the sun does; first the lower correspondences of the sun with the cosmos, then the higher "types" by which the sun reveals the Father of Greatness himself. The whole moves from natural appearances upward to the inmost mystery they signify, and then back outward to the daily showing of those mysteries in heaven for all to see.

The opening fragments set up the negative pole. The night shuts the eyes of all because Darkness fills the entire cosmos; her second evil is fear — when her shadow is manifested, fear and disturbance fall upon all men, and the cosmos is overwhelmed by the night. Read correspondentially, this is the operation of falsity-from-evil in the natural mind: where Light is withdrawn, the proprium asserts itself as a state of universal anxiety, the soul's natural reaction to severance from divine influx. The night is not only absence; it actively diffuses dread, because the natural recognizes, even in its blindness, that it has been cut off from Life.

Against this the sun is set forth in five works, which correspond to the complete natural-rational structure of the influx of Divine Truth into the cosmos. First, his light — he gives light to the cosmos and to all creatures within it: this is wisdom going out as truth into every receptive form. Second, his beauty — when he shines he pours forth beauty and uprightness on all things, which is the formative effect of truth conjoined with good, ordering and beautifying whatever it touches. Third, his peace — when the sun shines, men exchange greetings and give peace to one another: truth in the natural, when received, generates conjunction between souls, the social form of charity. Fourth, the life of the Living Soul — the sun habitually releases the Living Soul out of all the fruits and chains of heaven and earth: this is the redemptive heart of the sequence, Divine Truth in its illuminating manifestation actually loosing the dispersed light, the captured Living Soul, from its bonds in natural forms. Fifth, he gives power to the elements, and gives scent and taste to the whole Cross of Light: at the lowest pole, his influx animates the very ultimates, sweetening and quickening Divine Truth as it suffers crucified in the natural. So the five works of the sun are a complete arc: light, form, conjunction, liberation, and ultimate vivification — the five-fold descent of Divine Truth through every degree of receptive nature.

Each of these the teaching then declares to be exalted "beyond" — his light beyond all lights of the cosmos, his beauty beyond all beauties of men, his peace beyond all powers, his releasing far greater than all releasings, the power he gives to his members mighty beyond all powers. This "beyond" is the doctrinal hinge: the sun is not merely the chief among natural things, it is a sign whose meaning exceeds the natural register entirely. It points upward.

That upward pointing is then made explicit in three further "types revealed in the sun for the mystery of the first Greatness." First, the hiddenness of the disc of his stature: the sun's disc, hidden in its seasons, does not diminish — unlike the moon, whose disc waxes and wanes as it is filled. The sun's undiminishing fullness corresponds to the Father of the great Greatness, from whom all powers and gods come forth and who is never diminished, in whom no deficiency comes to be. The moon's mystery, by contrast, is the mystery of receptive reflection, of waxing and waning reception in the firstborn-state; the sun's mystery is the inexhaustible Source. Second, his light is exalted beyond all stars and all lights in the cosmos, corresponding to the mystery of the Father's own light, which is exalted beyond every particular truth and luminary. Third, the sun is raised toward the upper place of the All, beyond all mountains and hills, corresponding to the Father exalted in the upper place over all the heights of his Land of Light, hidden in his icon from eternity to eternity. Thus the three "types" — fullness, supereminent light, and elevation — are the three signatures by which the natural sun bears witness to the Father of Greatness as the Divine Esse: undiminished source, supereminent wisdom, and inmost height.

The teaching then turns to the larger frame: there are two mysteries, the mystery of the night and that of the days, which come forth daily in the cosmos. The mystery of the light and the mystery of the darkness are revealed daily in the creation of heaven; they are to be beheld as visions in their station. The first great light is the sun, the second luminary, who comes daily into the cosmos to reveal his graces and to manifest the sign concerning himself alone — namely, that he is unburied, one out of the substance of the unburied, who came forth from the unburied Father and has revealed himself in the cosmos. This is a precise theological statement: the sun corresponds to Jesus the Radiance, Divine Truth shining forth as Redeemer, of the same substance with the Father, sent into the cosmos to release captive light. The night, on her own part, exists as a shadow, corresponding to the mystery of darkness: she is the visible trace cast by the King of Darkness, recognized out of the cosmos through all its wickednesses.

The whole arc, then, is this. The Lord has so ordered the natural heavens that the daily alternation of day and night becomes a public catechism of the two essences. The sun teaches downward through five graces (light, beauty, peace, release of the Living Soul, vivification of the Cross of Light) and upward through three "types" (undiminishing fullness, supereminent light, exalted height) that the Father of Greatness is the unburied Source, and that his Radiance has come forth into the cosmos as the second luminary to release captive light. The night teaches, by shadow and by the fear it sows, that the realm of Darkness is its own substance, recognizable through all the wickednesses it generates. Both mysteries are shown daily, in the very creation of heaven, as visions to be read — so that no soul lacks a correspondential image, set in the sky itself, of the heaven from which it came and the hell from which it must be released.
